name: Payagua
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: La sílaba acentuada de los vocablos se indica por medio del acento agudo. [p. 255] // [Aguirre 1793, quoted p. 251:] Se detienen en las mismas sílabas de una palabra entonces mudan de tono, empiezan por bajo, suben luego y á la tercera toman el primero. [...] Las sílabas vocales tildadas son las que paran.
new_statements.translation: The stressed syllable of the words is indicated by means of the acute accent. // [Aguirre 1793:] They pause on the same syllables of a word and then change pitch: they begin low, then rise, and on the third [syllable] take the first [pitch] again. [...] The vowel syllables bearing an accent mark are the ones on which they pause.
new_statements.citation: Schmidt, Max. 1949. Los Payaguá. Revista do Museu Paulista, Nova Série 3: 129-269. São Paulo: Museu Paulista.
new_statements.locator: p. 255 (alphabet conventions preceding the 'Vocabulario de la lengua Payaguá', PDF p. 128); supporting quotation of Aguirre 1793 on p. 251 (PDF p. 124)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK. File (155 pp., BDCN scan of Revista do Museu Paulista N.S. 3). PDF p. 128 = printed p. 255: the sentence 'La sílaba acentuada de los vocablos se indica por medio del acento agudo.' is there verbatim, as the last line of the 'Consoantes' paragraph immediately before the heading 'Vocabulario de la lengua Payaguá / Apuntado en la Asunción en el año de 1940 con ayuda de la mujer Payaguá "María Dominga Miranda"'. Verified three ways: extracted text layer (reads 'sé' for 'se', an scanned artifact), the saved tesseract file, and a 110-dpi render of the page which I viewed (clean 'se'). PDF p. 124 = printed p. 251: the Aguirre 1793 quotation is verbatim, 'Se detienen en las mismas síla…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states a placement rule. Schmidt (the only linguist who recorded the language from a speaker, in 1940) marks the stressed syllable of every word with an acute accent, i.e. he treats stress as a lexical property to be listed per word. In his ~150 accented Payaguá forms (rough count from the scanned text layer) the marked syllable is final in about half (iguEslÉ 'forehead', irEpÉ 'neck', imahiÁr 'arm/hand', ivó 'foot'), penultimate in about a third (ivórü 'leg', yOlúgU, lOmilítik) and antepenultimate in the rest (siérAtA 'tooth', luguEchóhirA 'face', yukásAra), so stress is not fixed on any edge. Boggiani's earlier phonetic notation (per Koch-Grünberg 1903 p. 44) likewise marks 'Wortakzent' with an acute per word. Aguirre 1793 adds an impressionistic low-high-low pitch pattern over the syllables of a word.
new_statements.exceptions: None; no rule is stated, so no exceptions. Schmidt warns (p. 254) that his informant had largely lost the language and that its gutturals/nasals sounded weaker than in the 18th-19th c. accounts.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms of isolated words elicited in Spanish/Guaraní from the last speaker (Asunción, 1940); no phrase-level data.
new_statements.identity_note: Schmidt's 1940 data come from a single semi-speaker, María Dominga Miranda, in the Chorro/Tacumbú suburb of Asunción, i.e. the southern (Magach/Tacumbú) Payaguá remnant; Viegas Barros 2024 distinguishes two historical varieties (no separate glottocodes; language-level paya1236 only). Older lists (Aguirre 1793, Cerviño, Parodi 1888, Boggiani c. 1899) may represent the other variety.

sources.locator: p. 255 (alphabet conventions preceding the 'Vocabulario de la lengua Payaguá', PDF p. 128); supporting quotation of Aguirre 1793 on p. 251 (PDF p. 124)
sources.note: p. 255, orthographic conventions for his own 1940 data: 'La sílaba acentuada de los vocablos se indica por medio del acento agudo' -- stress is marked lexically with an acute accent in every word; no placement rule is given. p. 251 quotes Aguirre 1793 on syllable pitch ('empiezan por bajo, suben luego y á la tercera toman el primero') and 'Las sílabas vocales tildadas son las que paran'. p. 252 summarises Demersay: first syllables sibilant, last syllables short. Rough automatic count of accented Payaguá forms in the text layer: 50 final, 38 penult, 17 antepenult (scanned-limited).

sources.citation: Koch(-Grünberg), Theodor. 1903. Die Guaikurú-Gruppe. Mitteilungen der Anthropologischen Gesellschaft in Wien 33: 1-128 (Payaguá pp. 34-36; Boggiani's alphabets p. 44).
sources.note: No rule. Reproduces Boggiani's transcription alphabet for his Payaguá recordings, whose first symbol is the acute accent = 'Wortakzent' (word accent), i.e. Boggiani marked word stress per word; also quotes Azara, Aguirre and Demersay's impressionistic remarks on gutturals and on first syllables hissed / last syllables short and abrupt.
